angle: How draft-and-verify makes LLMs cheaper without changing outputs
linkedinPost:
Speeding up generation without changing what the target model would have said sounds like magic. It isn’t—it’s speculative decoding.

Definition: use a cheaper draft model to propose multiple next tokens; have the target model verify them in parallel, accepting matches and correcting when needed. Output distribution stays that of the target.

Baseline bottleneck: plain autoregressive decoding burns one target step per token and is often memory-bound, leaving parallel compute underused.

Mechanism:
- Draft proposals: a small model rolls out several candidate tokens ahead.
- Parallel verification: the target scores the proposed tokens at once, accepting matches.
- Corrective sampling: when a proposal fails, resample so the final text follows the target distribution.

Analogy: a fast apprentice writes ahead; a meticulous editor approves chunks or sends back specific fixes—final prose still reflects the editor’s taste.

Hypothetical deployment: speed up customer-email generation by 2-3x wall-clock on existing GPUs while preserving your approved target model’s behavior.

Tradeoff: verification costs apply to every proposed batch, not just rejects; net gain depends on acceptance rates and overhead.

My take: use it where outputs tolerate small stochastic variation but must reflect the same model. Measure acceptance, not just tokens/sec.

What’s your rule for turning speculative decoding on or off per endpoint? #ForwardDeployedEngineer #EnterpriseAI
xPost: Speculative decoding ≠ a new model. It drafts with a cheap model, then the target verifies every proposed token. Net speedup depends on acceptance rate and overhead, not hype. Preserve the target distribution or don’t ship. #ForwardDeployedEngineer
